title: Xavier Becerra Declared Winner of California Governor’s Race
description:
Xavier Becerra has been declared the winner of the California governor’s race, easily swatting away a challenge from Republican Steve Hilton.

	Bec
body:
Xavier Becerra has been declared the winner of the California governor’s race, easily swatting away a challenge from Republican Steve Hilton.

	Becerra, the Democrat, ran on a platform of lowering energy costs and working toward universal health care. The dominant theme of his campaign was opposition to President Trump, noting that he had sued the president more than 100 times as attorney general during Trump’s first term.


	After emerging as the top vote-getter in the June primary, Becerra had an easy path to victory over Hilton. He has made relatively few firm commitments — including on the issue of expanding California’s film and TV tax incentive.
	

	“Everyone recognizes that one of the reasons Southern California is such a destination point for tourists and people around the world is because of things like Hollywood, because of Universal Studios, Disneyland,” Becerra told Variety last month. “And so we have to fight to keep that industry here in Southern California.”

	Gov. Gavin Newsom announced a proposal on Monday to expand the state’s $750 million production tax credit to $1 billion, to include above-the-line costs, and to extend the sunset date to 2040. But Newsom will be out of office in two months, leaving any consideration of expanding the incentive to his successor.

	Many in Hollywood are pushing for an unlimited tax incentive, which would function as an entitlement and would not require discretionary approval from the state film commission. An Assembly special committee held a hearing on that issue last week, but the chair, Rick Chavez Zbur, said afterward that the  idea of an unlimited incentive is a “heavy lift.”
	

	Becerra has not taken a position on the issue, saying only that he wants to work to enhance the credit.

	“I’ll sit down with all the legislators to see what kind of proposals are put before us,” he told Variety. “But we’re going to fight.”

	Becerra’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment on Newsom’s proposal on Monday. Becerra posted a film policy on his website that did not lay out explicit commitments and that was rated by Pangram as 100% AI-generated.

	Becerra served in Congress before being appointed to replace Kamala Harris as the state attorney general. In the Biden administration, he served as secretary of the Department Health and Human Services. He emerged from a crowded primary field last spring, becoming the frontrunner only after Rep. Eric Swalwell was forced to withdraw and resign from Congress amid sexual misconduct allegations.

	His strongest Democratic opponent was hedge fund billionaire Tom Steyer, who had the backing of IATSE and a slew of progressive groups.

title: Democrats Win House, Poised to Take Senate
description: In an outcome seen as a backlash to President Donald Trump, Democrats were projected as easily capturing a majority of seats in the House of Repres
body:
In an outcome seen as a backlash to President Donald Trump, Democrats were projected as easily capturing a majority of seats in the House of Representatives in the 2026 midterm elections. Control of the Senate was still too close to call heading into the evening hours Tuesday, but Democratic candidates were leading in battleground contests.

	MS NOW called the Democratic flip of the House just before 10 p.m. ET, followed by CNN several minutes later, then NBC News and CBS News. The AP had not called the House race as of this writing.
	

	In the widely followed the Senate race in Texas, former state representative James Talarico was the projected winner over Ken Paxton, the state’s Republican attorney general. 

	“This is the repudiation of Trumpism that people have been hoping for,” CNN political commentator and former Obama adviser Van Jones said about the “Blue Wave” sweeping across the country. MS NOW’s Rachel Maddow said of the Democrats’ House win: “This is a seismic change in Washington.”

	The surge of support for Democrats comes as Trump’s approval ratings among American voters has plummeted over the course of the year, amid higher gas and grocery prices and the administration’s unpopular war with Iran. As of Nov. 3, just 37% of U.S. voters approve of Trump, near his lowest level ever of 36% just two weeks ago, per the New York Times’ analysis of multiple polls. Trump has stumped for Republican candidates at rallies across the country in recent weeks.

	With the Democrats retaking the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York’s 8th District, who is currently House minority leader, would be in line to become Speaker of the House.
	

	Among the other Senate races in contention in 2026, Democrats were ahead in several closely watched races Tuesday night, according to AP results.

	Those included Dr. Abdul El-Sayed vs. Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan; Sherrod Brown vs. Republican incumbent Jon Husted in Ohio; and Troy Jackson vs. Republican incumbent Susan Collins in Maine. In Senate races that were already called, Roy Cooper decisively beat Michael Whatley in North Carolina, and Annie Andrews prevailed in South Carolina over Darline Graham.

	If the Senate ends up with a 50-50 split between the parties, Republicans will have the edge as VP JD Vance would hold a deciding tie-breaking vote in the chamber.

	In gubernatorial races, notable Democratic winners Tuesday night included Keisha Lance Bottoms, who prevailed in the Georgia gubernatorial race, becoming the first Black woman governor in the United States. Amy Acton defeated former Republican presidential candidate and Trump ally Vivek Ramaswamy in the Ohio governor’s race, and Gina Hinojosa beat incumbent Texas Gov. Greg Abbott.

	Pictured above: James Talarico, Senator-elect of Texas

title: Weta FX and TAICCA Partner to Turn Taiwan Into an AI Screen Production Hub for Asia (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Weta FX, the New Zealand visual effects house behind “The Lord of the Rings” and “Avatar,” is teaming with the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAIC
body:
Weta FX, the New Zealand visual effects house behind “The Lord of the Rings” and “Avatar,” is teaming with the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA) on a plan to turn Taiwan into a center for AI-driven screen production in Asia.

	The partnership will be formally launched on Nov. 6 at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei. The launch takes place on the festival’s main stage right after the opening ceremony. The partnership will have three strands: joint investment, AI research and development, and training new talent.
	

	Specifics of the arrangement are being held back for the launch.

	TAICCA chair Sue Wang will appear at the event alongside three Weta FX executives: CEO Daniel Seah, chief technology officer Kimball Thurston and VFX supervisor Sheldon Stopsack.

	The pact pairs Taiwan’s AI and advanced-tech capabilities and its pool of creative talent with what Weta FX brings to the table – VFX know-how, a track record on international productions and a global network. The aim is to plug Taiwanese technologists and creatives into work across the worldwide screen business.

	For Seah, the deal carries a personal angle. He grew up in Taiwan. The studio has also been building ties on the island, appearing at the Taoyuan International Film & Technology Forum in August.

	The tie-up fits within TAICCA’s wider brief, which takes in the use of new technologies to make content. TTXC Innovations, a recently concluded market platform, is one case in point. It was built to help bring cultural content and tech to market by putting creators, tech developers, investors, buyers and distributors in the same room.
	

	Taiwan’s Ministry of Culture set up TAICCA in 2019. The agency backs Taiwanese content from development through production, distribution and overseas marketing, across film, TV, animation, publishing, comics, music, gaming and the performing arts. Its toolkit includes investment, co-production schemes, industry programs and partnerships abroad.

	Weta FX is based in Wellington, with outposts in Vancouver and Melbourne. It has won eight Oscars for visual effects, 17 Academy Science & Technology Awards, eight BAFTAs for special visual effects, 10 VES Awards in the photoreal feature category and five Emmys. Its latest work on the “Avatar” franchise was 2025’s “Avatar: Fire and Ash.” Titles in production at the studio include “The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum,” Marvel Studios’ “Avengers: Doomsday” and “Children of Blood and Bone.”

title: BAFTA Unveils 2026 Breakthrough U.K. Cohort, Including ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Star Ella Bruccoleri
description: BAFTA has unveiled its 2026 Breakthrough U.K. cohort, selecting 21 emerging creatives across film, television and games for its annual talent devel
body:
BAFTA has unveiled its 2026 Breakthrough U.K. cohort, selecting 21 emerging creatives across film, television and games for its annual talent development program, supported by Netflix.

	Now in its 13th year, the initiative recognizes rising talent across the screen industries, offering year-round career support, mentorship, networking opportunities and full BAFTA membership.

	Among this year’s honorees are actors Ella Bruccoleri (“The Other Bennet Sister”), Izuka Hoyle (“Prisoner”) and Sophie Stone (“Falling”), alongside filmmaker Myrid Carten, whose documentary “A Want in Her” earned acclaim on the festival circuit. The cohort also includes “Emmerdale” writer Yassmin Abdel-Magied, “Ish” director Imran Perretta and Louis Paxton, the writer and director behind “The Incomer.”
	

	In documentary and unscripted television, the program recognizes Chris Lynch, presenter and producer of “In the Driving Seat,” and Runako Celina, producer and reporter on “Death in Dubai.”

	Five creatives working in games have also been selected, including Eloise Singer, writer and director of “The Pirate Queen: No Safe Waters“; Husban Siddiqi, game director and developer of “Rogue Eclipse”; and Kate Killick, creative director of “Pieced Together.”

	“BAFTA Breakthrough is a hugely impactful programme,” BAFTA CEO Jane Millichip said in a statement. “It champions talented creatives and practitioners from all three screen sectors, and it is designed to give them the support and connections to build lasting careers.”

	The program’s alumni include Florence Pugh, Tom Holland, Jessie Buckley, Josh O’Connor, Bella Ramsey, Paapa Essiedu and Letitia Wright. Since its launch, more than 330 creatives have participated globally, collectively earning more than 200 BAFTA nominations and over 80 wins.
	

	Netflix returns as the program’s official supporter for the seventh consecutive year, with the partnership forming part of the streamer’s Generation N initiative to develop emerging and mid-career talent in the U.K.

	“We are so proud to back BAFTA Breakthrough for a seventh year,” Anne Mensah, Netflix’s vice president of U.K. content, said. “The group announced today is an incredibly exciting range of names, and it is an honour to help them flourish with the guidance and support this programme provides.”

	BAFTA North America is expected to announce its U.S. Breakthrough cohort later in November.

	Film


Hollie Bryan — Producer, “The Ceremony”
Louis Paxton — Writer/director, “The Incomer”
Lucy Allen and Tom Payne — Casting directors, “Sunny Dancer”
Imran Perretta — Co-writer/director, “Ish”
Regina Meessen — Hair and makeup designer, “Dreamers”
Ted Evans — Writer/director, “Retreat”



	Documentary/Unscripted


Chris Lynch — Presenter and producer, “In the Driving Seat”
Myrid Carten — Writer/director, “A Want in Her”
Runako Celina — Producer and reporter, “Death in Dubai”



	Television


Ella Bruccoleri — Actor, “The Other Bennet Sister”
Izuka Hoyle — Actor, “Prisoner”
Philippa Mumford — Production designer, “Juice” Season 2
Sophie Stone — Actor, “Falling”
Tom Cousins — Creator and executive producer, “Rafi the Wishing Wizard”
Yassmin Abdel-Magied — Writer, “Emmerdale”



	Games


Eloise Singer — Writer/director, “The Pirate Queen: No Safe Waters”
Husban Siddiqi — Game director and developer, “Rogue Eclipse”
Kate Killick — Creative director, “Pieced Together”
Niru Fekri-Arnold — Creator/designer, “Cursed Words”
Tom McKay — Performer, “Mysteria Ecclesiae: Kingdom Come Deliverance DLC”

title: Park Hoon-jung’s Assassin Noir ‘Tristes Tropiques’ Sells to North America, France, Spain
description: “Tristes Tropiques,” the latest genre outing from “New World” and “The Witch” director Park Hoon-jung, has been picked up for North America by Well
body:
“Tristes Tropiques,” the latest genre outing from “New World” and “The Witch” director Park Hoon-jung, has been picked up for North America by Well Go USA as Finecut, which is carrying the film in its AFM line-up, closes a fresh round of deals ahead of the film’s Nov. 25 theatrical release in Korea.

	Swift Distribution, whose president and CEO Didier Costet called the film “an exciting new cinematic journey,” has acquired French-speaking territories. Alfa Pictures will handle Spain and Andorra, Blue Swan Entertainment has Italy and CaiChang International, Inc. has taken Taiwan.
	

	The new pacts build on sales unveiled earlier to Splendid Film for Germany, Austria and Switzerland; Media4Fun for Poland; Multivision India for the Indian subcontinent; PT Prima Cinema Multimedia for Indonesia; and Izagur Media for Mongolia.

	The story centers on a band of young killers trained by Master, who holds absolute sway over a tropical rainforest. Then Master turns up dead. Nobody knows who killed him, and the assassins begin to distrust one another.

	The cast features Lee Sin-young (“Rebound”), Park Yu-rim (“Drive My Car”), Kim Myung-min (“Your Honor”) and Park Hae-soo (“Squid Game”). Taiwanese actors Austin Lin (“96 Minutes”), Chen Yi-Wen (“The Pig, the Snake and the Pigeon”) and Wang Po-Chieh (“Eye of the Storm”) are also part of the ensemble.

	Well Go USA has a track record with the filmmaker, having released “The Witch” films and “The Childe” in North America. Doris Pfardrescher, the company’s president and CEO, said: “We’re thrilled to continue our relationship with Park Hoon-jung. ‘Tristes Tropiques’ takes his signature blend of style, emotion, and hard-hitting action to a whole new level.”
	

	Park’s other credits include “Night in Paradise” for Netflix and “The Tyrant” for Disney+. Gold Moon Pictures, Park’s own company, produced the film, with Studio&New co-producing. Mindmark Inc., the Shinsegae Group’s creative content studio, presents.

	The film has already won over genre festivals abroad. The Brussels International Fantastic Film Festival gave it the Silver Raven Award from its International Competition, and in September Paris’ L’Étrange Festival named it winner of its Grand Prix Nouveau Genre Canal+. It has also been chosen to close the London Korean Film Festival.

	Finecut is also bringing animated feature “Long Long Night” to AFM, where an English-dubbed version will get its first market screening. The film’s festival run includes a Toronto Film Festival premiere and a Busan International Film Festival screening.

schema.headline: Park Hoon-jung’s Assassin Noir ‘Tristes Tropiques’ Sells to North America, France, Spain

title: ‘Dune 3’ Production Designer Patrice Vermette Created a 55-Ton Spaceship for Sci-Fi Epic: It’s a ‘Major Spectacle’
description: Production designer Patrice Vermette promises the third and final instalkment in the “Dune” franchise is going to be “a major spectacle.” “You know
body:
Production designer Patrice Vermette promises the third and final instalkment in the “Dune” franchise is going to be “a major spectacle.” “You know when you go see fireworks, and they put everything in, and at the end, it’s ‘Oh, we have this one.’ It’s going to be like that,” he teases.

	“Dune: Part Three” opens on Dec. 18. The film sees Timothee Chalamet return as Paul Atreides, continuing the story after his ascent to power at the end of “Part Two.”  Inspired by Frank Herbert’s novel “Dune Messiah,” the action takes place 17 years after the events of the previous film and explores the consequences of Paul’s rule as emperor. 
	

	Vermette was this year’s recipient of Variety’s Creative Impact Award presented at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival. During a conversation with Variety’s Senior Artisans editor Jazz Tangcay, Vermette was mindful about revealing anything too specific. 

	The one directive he had from director Denis Villeneuve was “not to repeat sets.” And he didn’t.

	Vermette shared some insight into how he pulled off the film’s opening sequence, which he says was a “crazy idea.” “The illustrations that I had made showed an expanse of black sand and ships attacking a planet.” One spaceship weighed 55 tons.

	“We needed to put it underground and bury it. For the whole scene, it rains. So, we had spider rigs and touch spinners, and it’s a big battle sequence. We only built one ship that you see the interior and exterior 360 degrees. Every two days, we had a crane during the day coming in, lifting it. And obviously, we had a pump system to take all the water out.” The results, he says, are “worth it.”
	

	Sharing their process, Vermette said, “The fun thing about working with Denis is we never want to repeat ourselves. Even though we’re in the same world.” They have a motto: “Let’s challenge each other. Let’s make it different.”

	Before getting into “Dune,” Vermette talked about getting his start in the industry working on music videos. He started collaborating with a director and realized he had found his comfort zone: “I understood the vision of the director.” It also gave him an adrenaline rush.

	As for working with Villeneuve, he and Vermette shared the same circle of friends and they had worked on commercials together in the early 2000s. The production designer was a huge fan, but their schedules never aligned for them to work together on a feature.

	“I was supposed to do ‘Dallas Buyer’s Club,’ and Jean-Marc Vallée tells me, ‘Patrice, that movie’s going to be pushed a year.’” When Villeneuve heard that, he sent Vermette a text.  Vermette recalled, “That text message changed my life.”

	The two were finally able to collaborate on the 2013 film, “Enemy,” Villeneuve’s first English-language movie.

	When Villeneuve proposed “Dune,” Vermette knew how much Herbert’s book meant to the filmmaker. “He started storyboarding for it when he was 15. He knew exactly where he wanted to be,” Vermette said.

	After receiving the first 100 pages of the script and revisiting the book, Vermette took plenty of notes. But he also knew from their collaboration that “things need to have a reason to exist. Whether it’s ‘Sicario,’ ‘Enemy,’ ‘Dune’ or ‘Arrival,’ it needs to tell a story. If it’s an object that exists in this fantasy world, it needs to be grounded in reality.”

	Discussing his process, Vermette explained it’s a collaborative process with other department heads, and together they figure their logistics out.

	“Dune” required Vermette to bring the planet Giedi Prime to life. For that dark, black world of the Harkonnens, industrial septic tanks served as inspiration. He also had to build the Atreides Castle, as well as the planet of Arrakis, where he built the Imperial Nexus Laboratory.

	Pulling off the lab was another challenge, but the collaborative process with cinematographer Greig Fraser and other department heads meant they could execute the scene without cheating sunlight. “Moral of the story: never give up on crazy ideas.”
	
	
		Artisans From ‘Obsession,’ ‘La Bola Negra’ and ‘Clarissa’ on Why Collaboration is the Key to Strong Filmmaking	

	If there is one takeaway from Variety’s 10 Artisans to Watch panel at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, it’s that collaboration, across all departments, is the key to strong filmmaking.

	“Our favorite films and TV series are not created by soloists,” Kathleen Radomski, Chair of Production Design at SCAD, said while introducing the panel. “They take a village. Departments and sub-departments, sometimes separated by thousands of miles, are all dedicated to a singular vision. This community is the height of collaboration and the essence of the entertainment industry’s massive global footprint.”

	Each year, Variety presents 10 artisans who use their varied skills to make an impact on their craft in recent movies and TV series. From big-budget blockbusters like “Project Hail Mary” to box office surprises like “Obsession,” the list celebrates talent from makeup, casting, editing, sound and music and more.

	This year’s recipients included Anne Jimkes, supervising sound editor of “The Mosquito Bowl”; Aulo Licinio, animation supervisor of “Project Hail Mary”; Landon Lott, art director and concept illustrator of “Pluribus”; Blair McClendon, editor of “Clarissa”; Adam Newport-Berra, cinematographer of“The Invite” and “Club Kid”; Raül Refree, composer of “La Bola Negra”; Jessica Ronane, casting director of “Elsinore”; Allie Shehorn, make-up and hair department head/ special makeup effects department head of “Obsession”; Grace Snell, costume designer of “Sense and Sensibility”; and Danny Vermette, production designer of “Backrooms.”

	The honorees joined Variety’s senior artisans editor Jazz Tangcay during the festival to break down their approaches to their respective projects and give advice to future filmmakers.

	Several panelists, including Lott, echoed Radomski’s sentiment about teamwork on “Pluribus,” especially when creating and designing the ice hotel, which drew inspiration from real Norwegian ice hotels.

	“There wasn’t just one person that designed this set,” Lott said. “There was a collaboration that went into it with not only the murals that were painted or carved on the wall, but with just the architecture in general.”
	

	Jimkes collaborated closely with “The Mosquito Bowl” director Peter Berg to balance loud sound and silence to make the film “as authentic as possible of an experience for both the actors and the audience,” she said.

	“It was essential that the audience was going to be in it and experiencing it along with the four main actors who portray these four real Marines or young men who back in the 1940s were all American football players,” Jimkes said.

	Strong collaboration also requires frequent communication. McClendon, who was attached to “Clarissa” before filming began — a circumstance he prefers — found his early involvement and open dialogue with directors Arie and Chuko Esiri to be quintessential to his editing process.

	“It was the kind of [shot] that I could only ask for because we had been talking about it for so long, and I was on it so early that I was like, “Oh, this is the exact kind of material in this thing that you’re going to want here,” McClendon said.

	Refree similarly got a head start on his score for “La Bola Negra.” Directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi came to Refree requesting composition “while they were writing the script because they wanted to get inspired by the music.” He also worked closely with Penélope Cruz, who has a large performance scene in the film. “I could see her building up the character, building up how that singer would be in the film,” Refree said.

	Ronane shared the same privilege of “building the world” when casting “Elsinore.” “We spend our lives interacting with actors,” she said. “I think everybody in the film I’ve seen on stage within the last two years. It’s a cast who are so well-placed to tell that story.”

	For Licinio, developing and animating a celestial being from scratch for “Project Hail Mary” was a bit more challenging. “We really had to work a lot into finding this personality of Rocky, ” Licinio said. “A lot of that came on set, a lot of mannerisms, a lot of little things.” After consulting the source material from the novel of the same name by Andy Weir, they referenced old slapstick movies and silent comedy legends Charles Chaplin and Buster Keaton to “see how body language would evolve into getting into performance.”
	

	While Rocky’s body language was a unique obstacle, one shared challenge some of these artisans faced was budgeting. “There’s this pie in the sky of what you want to do and then what you end up actually doing due to budgetary constraints,” Lott said.

	Shehorn approached makeup and gory visual effects in “Obsession” with that same practicality. “We only have so much money, so how do we pull this effect off collectively as a team using each department to make it look as realistic as possible?” she said. The result was only having two takes to get it right. “They couldn’t go back to like, ‘Okay, now let’s try it again from no blood,’” she added.

	For “Backrooms,” blood was not the problem, but “building the space, the sheer volume, was probably the biggest hurdle,” Vermette said. In fact, the team had to bring in a second rug that was a slightly different tone than the first because there simply wasn’t enough material. Vermette and director Kane Parsons ultimately adapted this restriction to be a symbolic transition in the film.

	Snell had to adapt historical garb in “Sense and Sensibility” for a modern audience: “If you’re not familiar with how [historical garments] are worn and put together, they’re sort of on a pedestal in a way. There’s a wall up somewhat because you don’t understand these garments and what they mean. So for how I could bring everybody in was if I did contemporary styling so that you could actually see yourself in these characters. How we might wear clothing today, which might be undone or somewhat mismatched, slightly self-styled,” she said.

	While they all had their unique challenges to overcome and different approaches to their individual tasks, each artisan concurred on the importance of collaboration, inviting emerging filmmakers to be kind and work together.

	“Think like a filmmaker,” Jimkes said. “You need to be able to talk to a producer in their language about budgets and schedules. You need to be able to talk with a director about the story. You need to be able to talk to your coworkers, for me, sound designers, composers, in their way of speaking, in their language. Be a filmmaker, learn about all the aspects. It’ll help you navigate the politics.”

	The only way to do so, Lott added, referencing Nike’s iconic slogan, is to “just do it”
	

	“Always be making shit,” Vermette echoed. “That’s a big part of it. Just keep going. Grab your buddies, go make a film. Just never stop. You don’t get good by sitting around wishing to be good. Just go out and practice, practice, practice.”

title: Kurosawa Award Winner O Mipo Is ‘Making Up for Lost Time’ After Career Break to Raise Her Sons
description: Co-recipient of the 2026 Kurosawa Akira Award together with Iranian filmmaker Mohammad Rasoulof, Korean-Japanese director O Mipo was in an understa
body:
Co-recipient of the 2026 Kurosawa Akira Award together with Iranian filmmaker Mohammad Rasoulof, Korean-Japanese director O Mipo was in an understandably upbeat mood when she met with Variety just before the award ceremony on Tuesday at Tokyo’s Imperial Hotel, under the aegis of the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival.

	The award honors filmmakers of substantial achievement who represent the future of cinema. O certainly fits that description: Since her industry start as a script supervisor for director Obayashi Nobuhiko, she has accumulated a long list of awards and accolades, beginning with a prize for her short “Eye” at the 2002 Short Shorts Film Festival in Tokyo.
	

	In 2005 her first feature-length screenplay, “The Sakai’s Happiness,” won the Sundance/NHK International Filmmakers Award. Based on this script, she directed her debut feature of the same title.

	In 2010, her drama “Here Comes the Bride, My Mom!” which she also scripted, won the grand prize for the Shindo Kaneto Awards, which are given to promising directors by a committee of Japanese producers. Her 2014 drama “The Light Shines Only There” was Japan’s submission for the Academy Award for best foreign language film.

	After releasing the 2015 drama “Being Good,” O stepped back from features to raise her two sons, though she directed a segment of the 2022 international anthology “Tell It Like a Woman.” She returned to features in 2024 with the coming-of-age drama “Living in Two Worlds” and followed with the 2025 eco-themed children’s drama “How Dare You?”
	

	“When I heard that they were going to give me the award my first reaction was just pure surprise – or rather, disbelief,” O says. “I couldn’t believe it. I wondered if they’d made a mistake. But I gratefully accepted it, of course. I hadn’t really made any big movies up to that point. I was just so happy that they found me out of all the (directors) in Japan.”

	The Japanese film industry, she says, is “overwhelmingly different” since she first entered the industry as a crew member in 1999: “There are a lot more female staff members now, and directors too. That’s definitely the biggest difference.”

	Also, what she describes as “the system for making movies” has changed. “Back in the day, the industry was like a pyramid, with directors at the top. That was my mindset, too, back when I was working as part of the crew.”

	Now, she explains, “It’s become pretty common for everyone to go through what you might call ‘respect training.’ In terms of rights, everyone is more or less on the same footing – or rather, in the same position.”

	But while production of Japanese films has been rising – nearly 700 are now released annually – O says she “can’t help but feel that the overseas market hasn’t really taken off yet.”

	“I have a desire for my films to be recognized overseas,” she adds, “but the Japanese films I always see at film festivals are just… a certain type. So I’d like to see many more films get that chance.”

	She would also like to follow in the footsteps of Kore-eda Hirokazu, Hamaguchi Ryusuke and other prominent Japanese directors who have made films abroad. “I’m thinking of giving it a shot myself,” she says. “I have a tremendous – call it ambition, or maybe just interest – to do that. I get asked that a lot: ‘What do you think of working overseas?’ I just come out and say, ‘I want to go to Hollywood someday.’”

	In addition to making movies, O has long worked as a director of TV commercials and makes no apologies for it. “I honestly don’t think there are any directors in Japan right now who are making a living solely from directing movies,” she says. “They have to do other things – like streaming, TV dramas, commercials, and all sorts of other work – because you really can’t survive just from movies.”
	

	“I’ve had a bit of a hiatus for about three years now because of raising my kids, but now that I’m back and have returned to filmmaking, the amount of time I have to devote to movies is enormous,” she adds. “When you’re making a movie, it takes up a huge chunk of your time. So even if I get offers for commercials, I have to turn them down. Gradually the number of offers dwindles and things have gotten a bit bleak since I’m relying solely on movies. I find that really ironic, though.”

	In Hollywood, she notes, directors are “usually paid a proper fee right from the planning stage, though I suppose it depends on the scale of the project. It’s part of the contract, but in Japan, the reality is that you don’t get a single yen at the planning stage. And that’s been the reality for a long time. I’m going through that kind of experience right now, too.”

	Turning to the subject of AI, she notes that it “has already become an inseparable part of our lives, and that includes filmmaking.” On whether machines will replace human filmmakers, she says, “I don’t think it will come to that.”

	“I tell my sons that it’s important to have a sense of self,” she adds. “To always keep asking yourself, ‘What do I think about this?’ – no matter what the situation is. Of course, it’s fine to consult with AI – in fact, doing so will lead to richer results. But I tell them it’s better to constantly keep asking yourself, ‘What do I really want to do?’ And I try to be mindful of that myself.”

	She takes inspiration from her mentor Obayashi, who started as a director of experimental films in the 1960s and went on to helm the cult sci-fi hit “House” and enjoy a long career mostly outside the Japanese industry mainstream. “He was always boldly taking on challenges,” she says. “It’s all about taking on challenges, right? It’s a constant battle but those challenges are like nourishment.”

	“‘House’ came out the year I was born – 1977,” she says. “That makes it a movie from nearly 50 years ago, but when young people watch it today, they’re absolutely blown away. I think it’s a film that will never lose its appeal.”

	That sort of longevity appeals to her – and not only for films: She notes that Obayashi died at age 82, Kurosawa at 88 and Shindo Kaneto – the scriptwriter and director whose eponymous prize she won – at 100.
	

	“I’m 49, so I still have half a century left,” she says. “Another 50 years, so I still have a long way to go. There was a gap in my career when I had children. But I’m making up for lost time. And with this [Kurosawa] award I feel I’m getting back on track.”

schema.headline: Kurosawa Award Winner O Mipo Is ‘Making Up for Lost Time’ After Career Break to Raise Her Sons

title: Lucy Liu’s ‘The Pirate Queen’ Expands With Graphic Novel, New Game and International Tour as Creator Eloise Singer Joins BAFTA Breakthrough Cohort (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Lucy Liu and Eloise Singer are preparing to take “The Pirate Queen: No Safe Waters,” their immersive experience about Chinese pirate leader Cheng S
body:
Lucy Liu and Eloise Singer are preparing to take “The Pirate Queen: No Safe Waters,” their immersive experience about Chinese pirate leader Cheng Shih, on an international tour next year, Singer tells Variety. The pair have also co-written a graphic novel and are developing a new game. 

	The news comes as Singer, the project’s writer and director, joins the 2026 BAFTA Breakthrough U.K. cohort.


	The franchise is built around a retelling of the stories about real life character Cheng Shih, who was a powerful female pirate in the South China Sea at the beginning of the 18th century.
	

	“No Safe Waters” played in the Cannes Film Festival’s Immersive Competition this year, with Liu narrating and producing alongside Singer. It follows the original 2024 VR version of “The Pirate Queen,” which earned an Emmy nomination.

	Liu says Cheng Shih was intelligent and strategically brilliant, and won respect through negotiation and leadership “in a world designed to exclude women entirely.” In Liu’s view, the pirate leader defies nearly every stereotype historically placed on Asian women in storytelling. “She was politically astute, ruthless when necessary, deeply strategic, and completely self-determined. Stories like hers remind us that history has always contained powerful, complex women – they were never centered in mainstream narratives,” Liu tells Variety. “That’s beginning to change, and I think audiences are hungry for stories that feel more expansive.”

	Where the first outing was built for a headset, the new piece fills a shared room with projection, sound and movement. Audiences stand among storms and fleets as dragons move beneath their feet.
	

	Liu does not appear on screen. She says voice carries a different kind of responsibility in immersive work, guiding atmosphere and movement at the same time. “In film, the camera captures a glance or physical gesture to communicate subtext, but here the voice can help create emotional architecture,” she says.

	Singer has spent a decade on “The Pirate Queen,” the last three years of it with Liu, and says the pair have co-written a graphic novel, are preparing the international tour and are developing a new game. “I feel really lucky to be making it with Lucy. She’s thrown her heart and soul into this alongside me, and getting to build this world together has been one of the most special parts of the journey,” she says. “I love seeing how one story can take on a whole new life across different formats, each offering audiences a completely different way to experience it.”

	Liu says the project’s ambition, and the importance of telling Cheng Shih’s story with nuance and scale, is something she and Singer both care about deeply. “We’re building ‘The Pirate Queen’ as a larger storyworld together, so it was never just about lending my voice to one experience,” she says. “As a producer, I wanted to help support the integrity of the story and the larger creative vision. I’m always drawn to work that challenges convention and creates space for voices and histories that haven’t been fully explored, and Cheng Shih’s story deserves that kind of scale.”

	BAFTA named Singer to this year’s Breakthrough program, its Netflix-supported initiative for emerging screen talent, on Nov. 4. She was selected in the games category for “No Safe Waters.”

	“It’s still a bit of a pinch-me moment. It’s something I’ve aspired to for such a long time, so to be selected is a little surreal, and to have BAFTA and Netflix recognize what we’ve created with ‘The Pirate Queen’ is incredibly special,” Singer tells Variety. “I’m especially proud that it’s for an immersive project. We started with a story we really believed in and wanted to bring it to life in a completely different way, something audiences could truly step inside and experience.”

	A friend who went through the program before her told her to make the most of every opportunity. “So that’s what I intend to do! I’m really looking forward to meeting other filmmakers and finding ways to take over the world together,” she says.
	

	Singer says this year is the first time she has really felt a scalable and sustainable future for immersive storytelling. “I’ve been genuinely encouraged by the level of distribution interest around ‘The Pirate Queen.’ It feels like there is a real appetite for immersive work now,” she says.

	Liu sees the form as both an extension of filmmaking and something new. “It grows from cinematic language but it also asks the audience to participate differently. That changes the relationship between story and viewer,” she says. “We’re still discovering the language of immersive storytelling which is what makes this moment so exciting creatively.”

	Singer’s background is in film and TV, and alongside new immersive work she is developing scripted projects. “I’ve always been drawn to stories about people who challenge expectations, whether they’ve been overlooked by history, underestimated by others, or simply refused to play by the rules,” she says. “Ultimately, I want to keep telling stories I really believe in and finding the most exciting ways to bring them to life.”

schema.headline: Lucy Liu’s ‘The Pirate Queen’ Expands With Graphic Novel, New Game and International Tour as Creator Eloise Singer Joins BAFTA Breakthrough Cohort (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Eric Dane’s Posthumous Memoir Reveals Actor’s Fight With Josh Duhamel on Set: ‘Let’s Go, You P—- Ass Actor!’
description: Eric Dane reveals in his posthumously-released new memoir “My Book of Days: A Memoir in Moments” that he fought with Josh Duhamel on the set of “La
body:
Eric Dane reveals in his posthumously-released new memoir “My Book of Days: A Memoir in Moments” that he fought with Josh Duhamel on the set of “Las Vegas,” the NBC series that Duhamel headlined opposite James Caan for five seasons between 2003 and 2008 (via Entertainment Weekly). Dane was a guest star on the show in Season 2 and filmed his episode while dealing with a herniated disc in his neck. As a result, he asked Duhamel to go easy on him while filming a fight scene.
	

	“We’re about to film a fight scene. I ask the lead, Josh Duhamel, to please not grab me by the tie during the scene. He promises me he won’t,” Dane writes. “The director calls ‘Action,’ and Josh pulls on my tie. Fire rips through my neck. I go, ‘Whoa, whoa, whoa, we have to stop.’ He apologizes, I grunt from the pain, and then, take two. He pulls on my tie again.”

	After two takes of Duhamel pulling on hist tie, Dane turned to a producer on set and warned him: “You better rein in your boy.” Duhamel then apologized for not listening and explained that he “got caught up in the moment.”

	“Fine. Okay. Take three, and son of a bitch, he grabs my fucking tie again,” Dane continues. “I whip off my suit coat and I say, ‘Let’s go, you pussy ass actor.’ I ball my hands into fists and I come at him. Nobody calls ‘Cut,’ the camera keeps rolling, and to the world who sees the whole nasty scene, I’m the aggressor, the hothead, I start the fight.”

	The incident was not Dane’s proudest moment on set. He writes later: “Josh and I have seen each other since and we’re cool. But I want to say it again. Josh, I was wrong. I should’ve walked away. I’m sorry, dude.”
	

	Dane guest starred on two episodes of “Las Vegas” in 2004, two years before getting his breakthrough TV role as Dr. Mark Sloan on the second season of ABC’s “Grey’s Anatomy.” Prior to “Las Vegas,” Dane worked steadily on television with guest roles on various series such as “Roseanne,” Married… with Children” and more. He also had recurring roles on “Charmed” and “Gideon’s Crossing.” 

	As for Duhamel, the actor revealed on “In Depth with Graham Bensinger” earlier this year that he could be tough to work during moments in his career where he would go to “pretty extreme places in my head” in order to tap into his characters. One such role was “Las Vegas” protagonist Danny McCoy, a former U.S. Marine dealing with PTSD while being the apprentice to a casino magnate.

	“When I got on set, people would be like, ‘Whoa, what the fuck is wrong with this dude?’” Duhamel said. “I was on the show ‘Las Vegas,’ and in the second season my character had gotten deployed to Iraq and he came back and he had seen some shit, and he was in a real dark place… That was the only way I knew how to do it, was to get into this place and stay there. [I] didn’t talk to anybody. I was just, sort of, in it. And people didn’t want to be around me. And people would, sort of, avoid me and it scared people a little bit, including me.”

	Dane’s memoir, “My Book of Days: A Memoir in Moments,” is now available for purchase.

title: Jennifer Lawrence Quotes ‘The Hunger Games’ While Urging Fans to Vote on Election Day: ‘Don’t Forget Who Burns With Us’
description: Jennifer Lawrence encouraged her 8.7 million Instagram followers to vote on Election Day by channeling her iconic role of Katniss Everdeen from “Th
body:
Jennifer Lawrence encouraged her 8.7 million Instagram followers to vote on Election Day by channeling her iconic role of Katniss Everdeen from “The Hunter Games.” The Oscar winner posted a photo of herself on Instagram giving the franchise’s trademark three-finger salute along with the caption: “Midterms [baby]. Don’t forget who burns with us. Go vote.” Lawrence included a link Vote.org, where people can look up their nearest polling location. 
	

	While Lawrence stopped short of endorsing any candidates, her “burn with us” quote comes directly from 2014’s “The Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 1” when Katniss fully embraces her role as a rebel leader against the tyranny of the Capitol (sound familiar?). After a hospital is bombed in her home district, an emotionally-charged Katniss gives a direct-to-camera address to President Snow and says: “You can torture us and bomb us and burn our districts to the ground. But do you see that? Fire is catching. And if we burn, you burn with us!”


	Again, Lawrence did not throw any direct shade at Donald Trump but her fans inferred as much given the symbolic nature of the “burn with us” quote in the “Hunger Games” franchise (and the deep ties between Snow and Trump). Lawrence was widely outspoken against Trump during his first administration as U.S. president, notably writing an op-ed after Election Day in which she declared that Trump’s victory meant “the only people that feel safe [in America], that their rights are recognized and respected, are white men.”

	However, Lawrence appeared to change course on getting political in media interviews when she told The New York Times last year on her “Die My Love” press tour that she was no longer sure she should speak out on Trump and politics.
	

	“As we’ve learned, election after election, celebrities do not make a difference whatsoever on who people vote for. So then what am I doing? I’m just sharing my opinion on something that’s going to add fuel to a fire that’s ripping the country apart. We are so divided,” Lawrence explained at the time. 

	She added, “I think I’m in a complicated recalibration because I’m also an artist. With this temperature and the way things can turn out, I don’t want to start turning people off to films and to art that could change consciousness or change the world because they don’t like my political opinions. I want to protect my craft so that you can still get lost in what I’m doing. And if I can’t say something that’s going to speak to some kind of peace or lowering the temperature or some sort of solution, I don’t want to be a part of the problem. I don’t want to make the problem worse… You watch these actors’ faces who have had incredible careers and made incredible contributions and then one half of the internet doesn’t want to see their face anymore. I get so upset for those people and it feels so wrong.”

	Lawrence has steered clear of political talk in interviews since then, although she made sure to encourage people to go vote on Election Day. Her decision to channel Katniss comes ahead of reprising the role in this month’s prequel movie “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”

	“It was unbelievable,” Lawrence said on the “Call Her Daddy” podcast last month about reprising Katniss after 11 years. “It was so crazy. It was the same crew. It was the same AD, who I’ve worked with a million times because I love him. And with Josh [Hutcherson] and Woody [Harrelson] … it was so emotional. Josh and I didn’t walk to the bathroom without our arms around each other. It was so beautiful. And Woody, obviously, came through the window of my hotel room uninvited. It wouldn’t be the same if he listened to boundaries or used a door.”

	“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” opens in theaters Nov. 20 from Lionsgate,

            TikTok star Marcel Johnson is dead after battling stomach cancer ... and social media is gutted by the tragic loss.
      
    
            His wife, Taylor, announced on Instagram that he'd lost his cancer battle on Monday in a heartbreaking post.
      
    
            She wrote ... "November 2 2026 @ 445pm. I lost a whole entire half of me. He fought so hard for so long. He was so tired & exhausted & in so much pain."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Taylor continued ... "Yesterday the only words Marcel said all day were to me & Dedric and it was 'I'm ready to go' and that was in the morning. He still fought to hang on all day so we just got a bit more time."
      

            She says she's struggling to process the devastating loss ... "I truly don't even have words right now. I feel like this can't be real life. How can this be real f***ing life. I thought I was going to wake up and he was still going to be here beside me."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Taylor concluded ... "I love him with my whole entire being and life will absolutely never ever be the same."
      
    
            Marcel -- a father of 5 -- was diagnosed with cancer last August, and has spent the past 15 months documenting his battle on social media.
      
    
            He was 32.
